title: References, values and object lifetime
description: Understand value types, reference types, and how long objects live in memory.

data.text: When you write `int x = 5;` in C#, where does the value 5 live? When you pass an object to a method, are you passing the object itself or something else? These questions touch on one of the most important concepts in programming: the difference between values and references, and how long objects stay alive in memory.

Value types hold their data directly. When you assign one value type to another, the runtime copies the entire value. Reference types hold a reference (a pointer) to data stored elsewhere — usually on the heap. When you assign one reference to another, you copy the reference, not the object itself. Both variables now point to the same object.

data.title: C# examples
items: int, double, bool, struct — value types
string, class, array, delegate — reference types
A value type variable contains the actual data
A reference type variable contains the memory address of the data

data.title: Value type assignment
data.content: Changing 'a' does not affect 'b' because the value was copied.

data.title: Reference type assignment
data.content: Both variables point to the same object, so changing one affects the other.

data.text: An object's lifetime is the period between its creation and its destruction. In managed languages like C# and Java, the garbage collector (GC) automatically reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable. You do not call delete or free — the runtime detects that nothing references the object anymore and cleans it up.

data.title: Reachability, not scope
data.text: An object survives as long as something can reach it. Even if a variable goes out of scope, the object lives on if another variable still references it.

data.title: Watch out for these mistakes
items: Assuming value types are always on the stack — boxing can move them to the heap
Holding references longer than needed, preventing garbage collection
Confusing string immutability with reference semantics
Modifying mutable objects passed by reference when you expected a copy

items.question: Are strings value types or reference types in C#?
items.answer: Strings are reference types, but they are immutable. When you assign one string to another, both variables point to the same string object until one of them is changed.

items.question: Does garbage collection run on a schedule?
items.answer: In C#, the GC runs automatically when it detects memory pressure or after a configurable amount of allocation. You cannot predict the exact timing, but you can influence it with generation-aware patterns.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Value types contain data directly; reference types contain pointers to data
Assigning a value type copies the data; assigning a reference type copies the pointer
The garbage collector reclaims unreachable objects automatically
Object lifetime depends on reachability, not just variable scope
data.takeaway: Understanding references and lifetime prevents bugs where data is unexpectedly shared or unexpectedly collected.
